clue.text: Shell of yellow car missing rear end

indicators.note: a thing missing its rear end has lost its final part, so the word for car is docked at the back

blocks.note: or is the heraldic word for gold or yellow
short for Mercedes, a make of car

explanation.surface: Someone describes the battered body of a yellow car whose back end has gone.
explanation.walkthrough: Heraldry gives OR for yellow; MERC loses its last letter to leave MER, making ORMER.
explanation.definitionFit: An ormer is an abalone, a sea mollusc prized in the Channel Islands, whose ear-shaped shell is lined with mother-of-pearl.

clue.text: Away? Ray is mistaken

blocks.note: off means away, as in 'she's off today'
a beam is a ray of light

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether Ray is away, and is told that is a mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ray' looks like a man's name, but it is a beam of light.
explanation.definitionFit: Off-beam is an informal adjective for wrong or inaccurate, like a signal aimed wide of its target.

clue.text: An adaptation of timeless Mountie film

indicators.note: an adaptation reworks its source material into a new form, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, fifteen letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A screen version of a classic tale about a Canadian Mountie that never dates.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface invites thoughts of a Mountie movie, but the two words are only raw letters for MEET ME IN ST LOUIS.
explanation.definitionFit: Meet Me in St. Louis is the 1944 Hollywood musical starring Judy Garland, so it is a film.

clue.text: Legal documents reportedly for luxury hotel

indicators.note: something reported is passed on by word of mouth, so the sound counts rather than the spelling

blocks.note: writs are formal legal orders issued by a court

explanation.surface: Court papers reportedly being served on behalf of a grand hotel.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ritz in London's Piccadilly is the archetypal grand hotel, its name a byword for luxury.

clue.text: Arrive and examine cabinet

blocks.note: to show, or show up, is to arrive
to case a place is to examine it, as a burglar does

explanation.surface: Instructions to turn up and inspect a piece of furniture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Show' for arrive is the informal sense, as in 'he didn't show'.
explanation.definitionFit: A showcase is a glass-fronted cabinet in which items are put on display in a shop or museum.

clue.text: One who's 11 and out?

blocks.note: surface reading: someone who is out of bed and about the house, yet also out of it
setter's reading: 11 across means on one's feet, and 'out' means unconscious, so a person walking about while fast asleep

explanation.walkthrough: The 11 refers to the answer at 11 across, UP AND ABOUT; being up and about while 'out', asleep, describes a SLEEPWALKER.
explanation.definitionFit: A sleepwalker moves around the house during sleep, on their feet but unaware of it.

clue.text: Other ranks locked in a row

indicators.note: something locked in is shut inside, so one piece is enclosed by the other

blocks.note: OR is the military abbreviation for other ranks, soldiers who are not officers
taken as written

explanation.surface: Ordinary soldiers are confined in a line.
explanation.walkthrough: The A sits inside OR. 'Row' looks like a noun, a line, but is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To oar is an old verb meaning to propel a boat with paddles, the same act as rowing.

clue.text: Crass, rude, misguided campaigners

indicators.note: something misguided is led astray, so these letters wander into a different order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A dismissive verdict on activists who are boorish and wrong-headed.
explanation.definitionFit: A crusader is someone who campaigns vigorously for a cause, from the medieval holy wars.

clue.text: Etonian, a monkey? One could make his teacher laugh

definitions.text: One could make his teacher laugh

blocks.note: a pupil at Eton, the English boys' boarding school
the howler is a loud South American monkey

explanation.surface: An Eton pupil is called a monkey, as a teacher might laugh at a cheeky boy.
explanation.walkthrough: Eton College is England's most famous public school, so an Etonian is a pupil there.
explanation.definitionFit: A schoolboy howler is a comic blunder in a pupil's work, the kind teachers collect and laugh at.

clue.text: Fed gruel that he prepared — that's to experience hardship!

indicators.note: food that is prepared is mixed and cooked, so these letters are worked into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, fourteen letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone is fed gruel cooked by a man, a sorry fate in itself.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface has the gruel already describing hardship, which hides that the words are the raw letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To feel the draught is an idiom for suffering financial strain, as if a cold wind were getting in.

clue.text: Pack some clothes to wear

indicators.note: some means only a part of what follows, so the answer is a run of letters inside those words

blocks.note: the run straddles the end of the first word, the second word and the start of the third

explanation.surface: Advice on packing a suitcase with a few garments to put on.
explanation.definitionFit: To stow is to pack or store something neatly away, as luggage is stowed.

clue.text: Girl in poem, Maud

indicators.note: in means contained within, so the answer lies inside the words that follow

blocks.note: the run spans the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: Pointing out the heroine of Tennyson's poem Maud.
explanation.walkthrough: Maud is a real Tennyson poem whose title is a girl's name, a ready false trail.
explanation.definitionFit: Emma is a common girl's name, and crosswords freely clue first names with 'girl'.

clue.text: Ready to start the day at college? An expert abroad

blocks.note: a student at university is said to be up
taken as written
a dab, or dab hand, is an expert
abroad can mean out and about, outside the house

explanation.surface: A student wonders whether an expert from overseas is ready for the morning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Up' for being at university, especially Oxford or Cambridge, is a British usage; 'dab hand' is everyday British for an expert.
explanation.definitionFit: Up and about means out of bed and active, ready to get going with the day.

clue.text: People of no importance making awful noise in tent

indicators.note: something awful is in a dreadful state, so these letters are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: taken as written, all three words

explanation.surface: Insignificant campers are kicking up a terrible racket under canvas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a placement instruction, but it is part of the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A nonentity is a person of no significance, literally a non-being.

clue.text: It carries letters about mother and the Italian coach

blocks.note: an informal word for mother
il is the Italian for 'the'
to coach is to train

explanation.surface: A railway carriage is shown carrying post, with mother and an Italian aboard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coach' looks like a railway carriage, which fits the surface, but it is the verb meaning to teach.
explanation.definitionFit: A mail train is a railway service that transports post around the country.

clue.text: Time to expect church working party

blocks.note: T is the standard abbreviation for time
to ask for something, such as trouble, is to invite or expect it
CE stands for the Church of England

explanation.surface: Announcing it is time for the church to expect a group of volunteers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Working party' reads as a church fete crew; 'party' here is a group, not a celebration.
explanation.definitionFit: A task force is a group set up to work on a specific problem, which is exactly a working party.

clue.text: Reject the Spanish weapon

blocks.note: el is the Spanish for 'the'
a bow fires arrows

explanation.surface: Someone turns down a Spanish arm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reject' looks like a noun but is the verb, from the British phrase 'give someone the elbow', to dismiss them.
explanation.definitionFit: To elbow someone is to push them aside or get rid of them, a figurative dismissal.

clue.text: Foundation school initially goes after scholars attached to one

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letter of the word it follows is kept
goes after means comes later in the line, so that piece is placed at the end

blocks.note: BAs are holders of a Bachelor of Arts degree
the Roman numeral for one
the opening letter

explanation.surface: Foundation school pupils start at the bottom, following the senior scholars.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Foundation school' reads as one phrase, but 'Foundation' is the definition on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: A basis is the underlying support or starting point on which something rests, its foundation.

clue.text: Reverse taxi up on to top of kerb

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means read from bottom to top, so the word runs backwards
the top of a word in a down entry is its first letter, so only that is kept

blocks.note: a cab is a taxi
the opening letter

explanation.surface: Instructions to back a taxi up on to the pavement.
explanation.walkthrough: A kerb is the British spelling of curb, the edge of the pavement.
explanation.definitionFit: To back a vehicle is to reverse it, both verbs for moving backwards.

clue.text: College girl from Norfolk town

blocks.note: King's College is in Cambridge (and in London)
a girl's name

explanation.surface: A female student arrives from a place in Norfolk.
explanation.walkthrough: Norfolk is a county in the east of England.
explanation.definitionFit: King's Lynn is a port and market town in west Norfolk, on the River Great Ouse.

clue.text: Inquisitive about e.g. a bouquet

indicators.note: about means around, so the first word goes around what follows

blocks.note: nosy means prying or inquisitive
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A nosy person asks questions about something like a bunch of flowers.
explanation.definitionFit: A nosegay is a small bunch of fragrant flowers, an old word for a posy or bouquet.

clue.text: Unstable African oil state

indicators.note: something unstable will not stay fixed, so these letters shift into another order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A volatile oil-producing country in Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests an African petro-state, but the state is American.
explanation.definitionFit: California is a state of the USA on the Pacific coast.

clue.text: Destruction caused by bug shaken off plant

indicators.note: something shaken off has been got rid of, so that word is removed from the larger one

blocks.note: bugloss is a bristly blue-flowered plant of the borage family
taken as written

explanation.surface: Crop damage is blamed on an insect that has been knocked off a plant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bug' looks like an insect pest in the surface, but it is literally the first three letters of BUGLOSS, which leave LOSS.
explanation.definitionFit: Loss can mean ruin or destruction, as in the loss of a ship or of life.

clue.text: Sunk low in river, first of piles

indicators.note: first of means the opening letter only of the word that follows

blocks.note: the Dee is a river in Wales, England and Scotland
the opening letter

explanation.surface: Bridge supports have sunk down into a river bed.
explanation.walkthrough: The Dee is a favourite crossword river.
explanation.definitionFit: Deep describes something lying far down below the surface, which is what sunk low means.

clue.text: This may be raised on board a ship from Qatar if a gunnel is damaged

definitions.text: This may be raised on board a ship

indicators.note: something damaged is knocked out of shape, so these letters are bent into another order

blocks.note: taken as written, fourteen letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A vessel out of Qatar might hoist a signal if its gunwale is broken.
explanation.walkthrough: A gunnel, or gunwale, is the top edge of a boat's side, which suits the nautical scene.
explanation.definitionFit: A quarantine flag, the yellow Q flag, is hoisted by a ship to signal it is under quarantine or requests clearance.

clue.text: Wine taster's difficulty

indicators.note: the possessive marks the letters as belonging to those words, so the answer is held inside them

blocks.note: the run spans the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A wine taster has a problem.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer sits inside the first two words; 'difficulty' is the definition, in the sense of a trap or snare one is caught in.
explanation.definitionFit: A net is a trap or entanglement, so to be caught in a net is to be in a difficulty.

clue.text: Insulating material, like finest found by sailor

blocks.note: as best means like the finest
OS stands for ordinary seaman

explanation.surface: An insulator as good as the finest, discovered by a seaman.
explanation.definitionFit: Asbestos is a fibrous mineral once widely used for fireproofing and heat insulation.

clue.text: Do some, but not all, by end of July

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only that is kept

blocks.note: part means some of a thing but not the whole
the final letter

explanation.surface: Instructions to complete some of a task, though not everything, by the end of July.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Do' looks like a verb, but it is the British noun for a social event.
explanation.definitionFit: A do is an informal word for a party or celebration, as in an office do.
